newsitem.title: UK: London gold at two-month low, but selling may be easing.
newsitem.headline: London gold at two-month low, but selling may be easing.

text.p: Gold prices fixed at a two-month low on Tuesday after tumbling below a key support level amid bruised market sentiment. In the morning, bullion fixed at $382.45 an ounce, a slide of more than $2 since the previous fixing on Monday afternoon and the lowest since July 9, 1996.
"Gold died, basically," one analyst said, referring to its slide below the important $385 an ounce support level in trading late on Monday in New York.
Market observers said further dips were possible.
"There is some support at $382 which may hold these initial tests, but obviously the big support it's going to go for is the July low of $380," said analyst Karen Jones of Credit Suisse.
But the market may have exhausted its selling potential for the time being, Jones and other analysts added.
Hectic selling in Asia early on Tuesday, which continued gold's decline, had appeared to ease off in Europe.
The afternoon fixing was 65 cents higher and by the London closing, prices had returned to the same ending level as Monday, $383.45.
"Now it should move sideways. I would have thought $381.50-$382 would be enough for the moment," a dealer said.
A brisk rally to around $386 an ounce was possible if players who had previously sold positions decided to buy back the gold, he added.
Sentiment was dampened last week by gold's failure to rally on strong U.S. jobs data and U.S.-Iraq tensions. Demand from jewellery makers was also low despite the end of the summer lull.
Dealers attributed at least part of the losses to renewed speculation about the International Monetary Fund's plan to sell part of its gold reserve to aid impoverished countries.
"That rather whipped the rug away from support which appeared to have been building at $385," a dealer said.

The IMF plan, due to be discussed at upcoming IMF and World Bank annual meetings, calls for the sale of about five million ounces of the IMF's 103.5 million ounce reserve to help finance its proposed Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF).
But IMF rules require 85 percent of the voting power of member countries before the gold can be sold, and some key members such as Germany still oppose the plan, say analysts.
Silver closed two cents up from Monday's London close at $5.11 an ounce, while platinum finished 25 cents lower at $393.50 per ounce.
Palladium probed its mid-August lows, finishing with a $1.80 loss at $122.95.
